```{r}
rating_data <- read.csv("Arena_raw_2026-09-25.csv")
price_data <- read.csv("OpenRouter_raw_2026-09-28.csv")[-398,]
#removing row 398 b/c it is the same model on a different mode
#Will eventually replace this step with a more all-encompassing method
rating_data %>% count(category, sort=TRUE)
```

```{r}
namecleaner <- function(x) {
  x %>%
    str_to_lower() %>%
    str_remove("^[^/]+/") %>%
   # str_remove(":batch$") %>%
    str_replace_all("[^a-z0-9]", "")
}
rating_data <- mutate(rating_data, modelname = namecleaner(model_name))
price_data <- mutate(price_data,modelname = namecleaner(id), is_batch = str_ends(id, ":batch"))
```
Batch models may not be included when doing actual modeling. 
```{r}
overall_ratings <- rating_data %>% filter(category == "overall")
english_ratings <- rating_data %>% filter(category == "overall")
non_english_ratings <- rating_data %>% filter(category == "non_english")
math_ratings <- rating_data %>% filter(category == "math")
coding_ratings <- rating_data %>% filter(category == "coding")
lit_ratings <- rating_data %>% filter(category == "creative_writing") 
```
I split each rating category into its own dataframe, but if it becomes necessary in the future they can be joined by model name if need be.
```{r}
head(rating_data, 5)
head(price_data,5)
```

```{r}
sum(is.na(overall_ratings))
sum(is.na(price_data))
```
There are a great deal of columns in price_data that have a bunch of empty entries.
I got rid of all columns that aren't pricing that contain more than 25% empty values, and then found some remaining
columns which I did not consider useful for analysis, so I removed them as well. 
```{r}
junkcols <- c("canonical_slug", "hugging_face_id", "supported_parameters", 
                    "default_parameters", "supported_voices", "knowledge_cutoff", 
                    "expiration_date", "links.details", "benchmarks.design_arena", "pricing.overrides",
              "alias_target.name", "alias_target.slug","original_json")
price_red <- price_data[, colMeans(is.na(price_data)) <= 0.25 | grepl("^pricing", names(price_data))] %>% select(-all_of(junkcols))
price_red
```

```{r}
merged <- price_red %>% inner_join(coding_ratings, by="modelname") 
overall_merged <- price_red %>%
  inner_join(overall_ratings, by = "modelname")
reduced_cols <- c("rating",
  "pricing.prompt",
  "pricing.completion",
  "organization",
  "rating_lower",
  "rating_upper",
  "variance",
  "vote_count",
  "context_length",
  "top_provider.max_completion_tokens",
  "license",
  "created")
merged_red <- merged %>% select(all_of(reduced_cols)) %>% mutate(input_price = pricing.prompt*1000000, output_price = pricing.completion*1000000) %>% mutate(mixed_price = ((4*input_price + output_price)/5), log_price = log(mixed_price))
#log2_price = log2(mixed_price)
corrplot::corrplot(cor(select(merged_red, c("log_price", "created", "context_length", 
                             "top_provider.max_completion_tokens", "vote_count"))),method="number")

```

```{r}
hist(merged_red$pricing.prompt,breaks=30)
hist(merged_red$pricing.completion, breaks=30)
plot(merged_red$pricing.prompt, merged$pricing.completion)
```
Most models are rather cheap. A few are pricier. Does organization and license
influence these trends?
```{r}
plot(log(merged$pricing.prompt), merged$rating)
plot(log(merged$pricing.completion), merged$rating)
plot(merged_red$log_price, merged_red$rating, )

```
There appears to be a positive correlation between pricing and rating. 
Completion price appears more correlated with rating than prompt price,
which makes sense. Completion price represents the price of the actual
response of the LLM. 

Let's see if it holds up in simple regression. 
```{r}
model_completion <- lm(log(pricing.completion) ~ rating, data= merged)
summary(model_completion)
```
The correlation is not very strong, but it is positive and highly significant. 

```{r}
model_prompt <- lm(log_price ~ rating, data= merged_red)
summary(model_prompt)
```
```{r}
#Predicting price based on features
model_mult_price <- lm(log_price ~ rating + created + context_length + top_provider.max_completion_tokens
                 + vote_count, data = merged_red)
summary(model_mult_price)

#Predicting rating based on features
model_mult_rating <- lm(rating ~ log_price + created + context_length + top_provider.max_completion_tokens
                 + vote_count, data = merged_red)
summary(model_mult_rating)
```
While our model predicts price at only a weak-to-moderate level, using linreg
to predict rating gives quite successful results. 

From here, it is best to try and incorporate our categoricals. Let's do some
exploration of them, first:
```{r}
ggplot(merged_red, aes(x = reorder(organization, log_price, FUN = mean), 
                       y = log_price, fill = organization)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Value Distribution Across Groups", x = "Firm", 
       y = "mixed price (USD per 1M tokens)") +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "none")

ggplot(merged_red, aes(x = reorder(organization, rating, FUN = mean), 
                       y = rating, fill = organization)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Value Distribution Across Groups", x = "Firm", 
       y = "rating") +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "none")

```
